I have come, I am here

I have come, I am here. It differs from ἔρχεσθαι [to come] and ἱκνεῖσθαι [to arrive], which have the simple meaning of coming: but ἥκειν [to have come] contains a double notion, to have come and to be present. Only three tenses are in use, the present ἥκω, the imperfect ἧκον and the future ἥξω.
Imperfect
Future
With the accusative without a preposition.
concerning the Palici

Thus in Macrobius Sat. 5, 19, whose best manuscript has ἵκουσ' [they came], which might seem to be used because of the etymology of the name Παλικῶν [of the Palici]. But the sense rather requires the future ἥξουσ' [they will come], which Burges restored.
Porson for ἵκετε [you came].
Thus Hermann for ἠρκέσω [you ruled].
where ἥξω [I will come] is suspected, changed by Auratus to ἄξω [I will lead], by Schneidewin to τάξω [I will arrange]. To Weil three verses before ἥξω seem to have fallen out.
